strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: Prior distractor-free datasets (5-12 scenes) have become saturated despite rapid research growth (~2× papers in 2025), making this ~100× scale-up meaningful and timely

Substantial scale and diversity: 1,048 scenes with 128 distractor types and 161 themes, collected over 9 months across 12 devices and 9 resolutions—far exceeding prior work (RobustNeRF: 5 scenes, 4 types; On-the-go: 12 scenes, 14 types)

Systematic dataset design: Well-documented pipeline (Fig. 6) with manual review, COLMAP verification, instant-ngp validation, and DF3DV-41 curated subset with 17 targeted scenarios for granular evaluation

Comprehensive benchmark: Evaluates 10 methods across all scenes, revealing meaningful performance progression aligned with publication timeline and identifying specific failure modes (semantically-similar distractors, fluid phenomena, nighttime scenes)
Demonstrates practical utility: DI2FIX application with systematic ablations (Tables 5-6) shows importance of scale/diversity; out-of-distribution testing (Table S.5) validates generalization

Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-organized writing, detailed methods, honest limitation discussion, and sufficient detail for reproduction; enables 'zoom-in no more' visual comparisons where method differences are directly observable
weaknesses: Limited scale relative to modern standards: 1,048 scenes remains modest compared to general vision datasets (10K+), and acknowledged higher capture costs may limit further growth; risk of saturation similar to predecessors as methods improve

Modest methodological novelty: Data collection is straightforward (consumer cameras, manual protocols); benchmark uses standard metrics; DI2FIX is direct adaptation of existing DIFIX framework; no novel techniques for addressing distractor-free challenges

Underdeveloped application: DI2FIX shows only 0.96 dB PSNR and 0.057 LPIPS gains on limited metrics (SSIM changes 'relatively limited'), tested on single base framework; authors label as 'pilot experiment' and acknowledge confirmation bias issues (Fig. S.14)

Data quality concerns: Acknowledged 'slight cloud movement' in clean images despite short capture; manual separation of clean/cluttered for uncontrollable scenes introduces error; no inter-rater reliability analysis or systematic bias assessment

Shallow failure analysis: Benchmark identifies challenging scenarios but offers limited mechanistic insight; observation that semantic methods fail on semantically-similar distractors is somewhat predictable; limited guidance for future method development

Narrow generalization scope: All casual handheld capture with consumer cameras; unclear generalization to professional capture, aerial/robotic systems, or other domains; single data distribution limits applicability beyond this specific task

Incomplete comparative analysis: Concurrent works (RealX3D, D-RE10K-iPhone) unpublished at submission; leave-one-method-out tests only unseen distractor-free methods; no cross-dataset generalization study (e.g., DF3DV-trained models on On-the-go)

Unclear distractor taxonomy: 128 types seem comprehensive but taxonomy construction process not detailed; how were categories defined and validated? Potential for subjective or redundant categorization not addressed
